title: Part 1, Chapter 31
paragraphs: About the delightful conversation between Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, his squire, together with other incidents

"None of that is unsatisfactory to me," said Don Quixote. "Go on; you reached her — and what was that queen of beauty doing? Surely you found her stringing pearls, or embroidering some device in gold thread for this her enslaved knight."
"I didn't," said Sancho. "I found her winnowing two bushels of wheat in the yard of her house."
"Then depend on it," said Don Quixote, "the grains of that wheat were pearls when touched by her hands. And did you look, friend? Was it white wheat or brown?"
"It was neither — it was red," said Sancho.

"Then I promise you," said Don Quixote, "that, winnowed by her hands, beyond a doubt the bread it made was of the whitest. But go on; when you gave her my letter, did she kiss it? Did she place it on her head? Did she perform any ceremony worthy of it, or what did she do?"

"When I went to give it to her," replied Sancho, "she was hard at it, swaying from side to side with a lot of wheat she had in the sieve, and she said to me, 'Lay the letter, friend, on top of that sack, for I can't read it until I've finished sifting all this.'"

"Discreet lady!" said Don Quixote. "That was so she could read it at her leisure and enjoy it. Go on, Sancho — while she was busy with her work, what conversation did she hold with you? What did she ask about me, and what did you answer? Hurry up; tell me everything, and let not an atom be left in the ink-bottle."

"She asked me nothing," said Sancho. "But I told her how your worship was left doing penance in her service, naked from the waist up, in among these mountains like a savage, sleeping on the ground, not eating bread off a tablecloth nor combing your beard, weeping and cursing your fortune."

"In saying I cursed my fortune you said wrong," said Don Quixote. "Rather, I bless it, and shall bless it all the days of my life for having made me worthy of aspiring to love so lofty a lady as Dulcinea del Toboso."
"And so lofty she is," said Sancho, "that she stands more than a hand's-breadth taller than I am."
"What? Sancho," said Don Quixote, "did you measure yourself against her?"
"I measured this way," said Sancho. "Going to help her put a sack of wheat on the back of an ass, we came so close together that I could see she stood more than a good palm over me."

"Well!" said Don Quixote. "And does she not in truth accompany and adorn this stature with a thousand million charms of mind? But one thing you will not deny, Sancho — when you came close to her, did you not catch a Sabaean fragrance, an aromatic scent, a — I know not what — something delicious that I cannot name; a redolence, an exhalation, as if you were in the shop of some fine glover?"
"All I can say," said Sancho, "is that I did catch a little odour, something goatish — it must have been that she was all in a sweat with hard work."

"It cannot be that," said Don Quixote. "You must have had a cold in the head, or smelled yourself; for I know well what would be the scent of that rose among thorns, that lily of the field, that dissolved amber."
"Maybe so," replied Sancho. "There often comes from me that same odour which then seemed to me to come from her grace the lady Dulcinea; but that's no wonder — one devil is like another."
"Well then," Don Quixote continued, "now she has finished sifting the corn and sent it to the mill — what did she do when she read the letter?"

"As for the letter," said Sancho, "she didn't read it, because she said she could neither read nor write. Instead she tore it up into small pieces, saying she didn't want to let anyone read it for fear her secrets might be known in the village, and that what I had told her by word of mouth about the love your worship bore her, and the extraordinary penance you were doing for her sake, was enough; and, to make an end of it, she told me to tell your worship that she kissed your hands, and that she had a greater desire to see you than to write to you; and that therefore she begged and commanded you, on sight of this present message, to come out of these thickets and have done with carrying on absurdities, and to set out at once for El Toboso — unless something more important came up — for she had a great longing to see your worship. She laughed a great deal when I told her how your worship was called the Knight of the Rueful Countenance. I asked her if that Biscayan from the other day had been there, and she told me he had, and that he was an honest fellow; I asked her too about the galley slaves, but she said she had not seen any as yet."

"So far so good," said Don Quixote. "But tell me, what jewel did she give you on taking your leave, in return for your news of me? It's a customary and ancient practice with knights and ladies errant to give the squires, damsels, or dwarfs who bring tidings of their ladies to the knights, or of their knights to the ladies, some rich jewel as a reward for good news and acknowledgement of the message."

"That sounds very likely," said Sancho, "and a good custom too, to my mind; but that must have been in days gone by, because nowadays it seems the custom is to give only a piece of bread and cheese — which is what my lady Dulcinea gave me over the top of the yard-wall when I took leave of her. And, for added proof, it was sheep's-milk cheese."

"She is generous in the extreme," said Don Quixote, "and if she didn't give you a jewel of gold, no doubt it was because she didn't have one to hand to give you; but sleeves are good after Easter — I shall see her and all will be put right. But do you know what amazes me, Sancho? It seems to me you must have gone and come through the air, since you took little more than three days to go to El Toboso and return, even though it's more than thirty leagues from here to there. From which I'm inclined to think that the sage magician who is my friend, and watches over my interests (for there must necessarily be such a one, or else I wouldn't be a true knight-errant) — that this same magician, I say, must have helped you travel without your knowing it. Because some of these sages will catch up a knight-errant sleeping in his bed, and without his knowing how or in what way it happened, he wakes up the next day more than a thousand leagues from where he went to sleep. If it weren't for this, knights-errant could not come to one another's aid in peril, as they do at every turn. A knight, say, is fighting in the mountains of Armenia with some dragon, or fierce serpent, or another knight, and gets the worst of the battle, and is at the point of death; but when he least expects it, there appears across from him on a cloud, or chariot of fire, another knight, a friend of his, who just before had been in England, who takes his side and saves him from death; and at night he finds himself in his own quarters, supping very much to his satisfaction; and yet from one place to the other will have been two or three thousand leagues. All this is done by the craft and skill of the sage enchanters who take care of those valiant knights; so, friend Sancho, I have no difficulty in believing that you may have gone from this place to El Toboso and returned in such a short time, since, as I have said, some friendly sage must have carried you through the air without your noticing."
"That must have been it," said Sancho, "because Rocinante really did go like a gypsy's ass with quicksilver in his ears."

"Quicksilver!" said Don Quixote. "Yes, and what is more, a legion of devils — folk that can travel and make others travel without weariness, exactly as the whim takes them. But setting this aside, what do you think I should do about my lady's command to go and see her? Because, while I feel I am bound to obey her order, I feel too that I'm prevented by the boon I have granted to the princess accompanying us, and the law of chivalry compels me to honour my word in preference to my inclination. On the one hand, the desire to see my lady pursues and harasses me; on the other, my solemn promise and the glory I'll win in this enterprise urge and call to me. But what I think I'll do is travel with all speed and reach the place where this giant is as soon as possible, and on my arrival I'll cut off his head and settle the princess peacefully in her realm, and then immediately return to behold the light that illuminates my senses, to whom I will make such excuses that she'll be led to approve of my delay, since she will see that it entirely tends to increase her glory and fame — for all that I have won, am winning, or shall win by arms in this life, comes to me by the favour she extends to me, and because I am hers."

"Oh, what a sad state your worship's brains are in!" said Sancho. "Tell me, señor, do you mean to travel all that way for nothing, and to let slip and lose so rich and grand a match as this — where they give as a dowry a kingdom that in sober truth I have heard is more than twenty thousand leagues around, and abounds with everything necessary to support human life, and is bigger than Portugal and Castile put together? Peace, for the love of God! Blush for what you've said, and take my advice, and forgive me, and marry at once in the first village where there's a curate; if not, here's our licentiate, who will do the job beautifully. Remember, I'm old enough to give advice, and this advice comes pat to the purpose — for a sparrow in the hand is better than a vulture on the wing, and he who has the good in his hand and chooses the bad has no right to complain when the good doesn't come to him."

"Look here, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "If you're advising me to marry so that immediately upon killing the giant I'll become king and be able to confer favours on you and give you what I have promised — let me tell you I shall be able to satisfy your desires very easily without marrying; for before going into battle I'll make it a condition that, if I come out of it victorious, even if I don't marry, they shall give me a portion of the kingdom so I may bestow it on whomever I choose; and when they give it to me, on whom would you have me bestow it but you?"

"That's plain speaking," said Sancho. "But let your worship take care to choose it on the seacoast, so that if I don't like the life, I can ship off my black vassals and deal with them as I've said. Don't mind going to see my lady Dulcinea now — go and kill this giant and let's finish off this business; for by God it strikes me it will be a matter of great honour and great profit."

"I hold that you're right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and I'll take your advice about accompanying the princess before going to see Dulcinea. But I caution you not to say anything to anyone, including those who are with us, about what we have considered and discussed. Since Dulcinea is so discreet that she does not want her thoughts known, it is not right that I, or anyone on my behalf, should disclose them."

"Well then, if that's the case," said Sancho, "how is it that your worship makes everyone you defeat by your arm go and present themselves before my lady Dulcinea — which is the same as signing your name to it that you love her and are her lover? And since those who go must kneel before her and say they come from your worship to submit themselves to her, how can the thoughts of either of you be hidden?"

"Oh, how foolish and simple you are!" said Don Quixote. "Don't you see, Sancho, that this only adds to her greater glory? You must know that, according to our way of thinking in chivalry, it's a high honour to a lady to have many knights-errant in her service, whose thoughts go no further than serving her for her own sake, and who look for no other reward for their great and true devotion than that she should be willing to accept them as her knights."

"It's with that kind of love," said Sancho, "that I have heard preachers say we ought to love our Lord — for himself alone, without being moved by the hope of glory or the fear of punishment; though for my part, I would rather love and serve him for what he could do."
"The devil take you for a clown!" said Don Quixote. "What shrewd things you say at times! One would think you'd studied."
"In faith, then, I cannot even read."

Master Nicholas called out to them at this point to wait a while, as they wanted to stop and drink at a little spring there was nearby. Don Quixote drew up, much to the satisfaction of Sancho, who by this time was weary of telling so many lies and afraid his master would catch him tripping; for though he knew that Dulcinea was a peasant girl of El Toboso, he had never seen her in his life. Cardenio had now put on the clothes Dorothea was wearing when they found her, and though they weren't very good, they were far better than the ones he took off. They dismounted together by the side of the spring, and with what the curate had provided himself with at the inn they appeased, though not very well, the keen appetite they had all brought with them.

While they were so occupied, a youth happened to come by on his way along the road; stopping to examine the party at the spring, the next moment he ran to Don Quixote and, clasping him around the legs, began to weep freely, saying, "Oh, señor, do you not know me? Look at me well; I am that lad Andrés that your worship released from the oak-tree where I was tied."

Don Quixote recognised him, and taking his hand, he turned to those present and said: "So that your worships may see how important it is to have knights-errant in the world to redress the wrongs and injuries done by tyrannical and wicked men, I tell you that some days ago, passing through a wood, I heard cries and pitiful complaints as of a person in pain and distress; I immediately hurried, driven by my bounden duty, to the quarter from which the plaintive sounds seemed to come, and I found this lad now before you tied to an oak — which I rejoice at in my heart, for his testimony will not permit me to depart from the truth in any particular. He was, I say, tied to an oak, naked from the waist up, and a clown, whom I later found to be his master, was scoring him with lashes from the reins of his mare. As soon as I saw him I asked the reason for so cruel a flogging. The boor replied that he was flogging him because he was his servant, and because of carelessness that proceeded more from dishonesty than stupidity; at which this boy said, 'Señor, he flogs me only because I ask for my wages.' The master made I-don't-know-what speeches and explanations, which, though I listened, I didn't accept. In short, I forced the clown to unbind him and to swear he would take him with him and pay him real by real, and perfumed into the bargain. Isn't that all true, Andrés my son? Didn't you notice with what authority I commanded him, and with what humility he promised to do all I enjoined, specified, and required of him? Answer without hesitation; tell these gentlemen what took place, so they may see that it's as great an advantage as I say to have knights-errant abroad."
"All that your worship has said is quite true," answered the lad, "but the end of the business turned out just the opposite of what your worship supposes."
"What? The opposite?" said Don Quixote. "Did the clown not pay you, then?"

"Not only did he not pay me," replied the lad, "but as soon as your worship had passed out of the wood and we were alone, he tied me up again to the same oak and gave me a fresh flogging that left me like a flayed Saint Bartholomew; and every stroke he gave me he followed up with some joke or jeer about having made a fool of your worship — and but for the pain I was in, I should have laughed at the things he said. In short, he left me in such a state that I have been until now in a hospital getting cured of the injuries that rascally clown inflicted on me then — for which your worship is to blame. Because if you had gone your own way and not come where there was no call for you, nor meddled in other people's affairs, my master would have been content with giving me one or two dozen lashes and would then have untied me and paid me what he owed me. But when your worship abused him so out of all measure and gave him so many hard words, his anger was kindled; and since he couldn't take revenge on you, as soon as he saw you had left him, the storm burst on me in such a way that I feel I shall never be a man again."

"The mischief," said Don Quixote, "lay in my going away; for I should not have gone until I had seen you paid. Because I ought to have known well by long experience that there is no clown who will keep his word if he finds it doesn't suit him to keep it. But you remember, Andrés, that I swore if he didn't pay you I would go and seek him and find him, even if he hid himself in the whale's belly."
"That's true," said Andrés, "but it was no use."

"You shall see now whether it's of use or not," said Don Quixote. And so saying, he got up hastily and told Sancho to bridle Rocinante, who was grazing while they ate. Dorothea asked him what he meant to do. He replied that he meant to go in search of this clown and chastise him for such wicked conduct, and see Andrés paid to the last maravedí, in spite of all the clowns in the world. To which she replied that he must remember that, in accordance with his promise, he could not undertake any enterprise until he had finished hers; and that since he knew this better than anyone, he should restrain his ardour until his return from her kingdom.
"That's true," said Don Quixote, "and Andrés must have patience until my return, as you say, señora; but I once more swear and promise not to stop until I have seen him avenged and paid."

"I have no faith in those oaths," said Andrés. "I would rather have something now to help me get to Seville than all the revenges in the world. If you have anything to eat that I can take with me, give it to me, and God be with your worship and all knights-errant; and may their errands turn out as well for themselves as they have for me."
Sancho took a piece of bread and another of cheese out of his store and, giving them to the lad, said, "Here, take this, brother Andrés, since we all of us have a share in your misfortune."
"Why — what share have you got?"

"This share of bread and cheese I'm giving you," answered Sancho, "and God knows whether I shall feel the want of it myself or not. I'll have you know, friend, that we squires to knights-errant have to bear a great deal of hunger and hard fortune, and other things too more easily felt than told."

Andrés seized his bread and cheese, and seeing that nobody gave him anything more, bent his head and took to the road, as the saying is. Before leaving, however, he said, "For the love of God, sir knight-errant, if you ever meet me again, even if you see them cutting me to pieces, give me no aid or help, but leave me to my misfortune — which will not be so great but that a greater will come to me by being helped by your worship, on whom, and on all the knights-errant ever born, God send his curse."

Don Quixote was getting up to chastise him, but he took to his heels at such a pace that no one tried to follow him; and mightily crestfallen was Don Quixote at Andrés's story, and the others had to take great care to restrain their laughter so as not to put him entirely out of countenance.
